title: Passive verbs (이/히/리/기)
plainEnglish: Turns an action verb into a passive one, so the subject has something done to it instead of doing it.
whenToUse: Reach for this when the spotlight is on what HAPPENS to the subject, and the doer is unknown, obvious, or simply not the point — a door that won't open (문이 안 열려요), sound that carries through a wall (소리가 들려요), food that sells out (다 팔렸어요), or you getting bitten (모기한테 물렸어요). It is the everyday voice of complaints, signs, and apartment-life grumbling, where you'd sound stiff naming an agent. 피동(被動) literally means 'receive-move', i.e. the subject RECEIVES the action. Note this set is the lexical (built-in) passive that lives inside specific verbs — you can't apply it freely; you pick from a memorized list. When you really must name who did it, drop in 에게/한테 for a person or 에 for a force (소나기에 옷이 젖었어요 = my clothes got soaked in the rain shower).
attachmentRule: Insert one of -이-/-히-/-리-/-기- between the verb stem and the ending; which one is fixed per verb and must be memorized. -이-: 보다→보이다 (be seen), 놓다→놓이다, 쌓다→쌓이다. -히-: 닫다→닫히다 (be closed), 먹다→먹히다, 잡다→잡히다, 막다→막히다. -리-: 열다→열리다 (be opened), 듣다→들리다 (be heard), 팔다→팔리다, 밀다→밀리다. -기-: 안다→안기다, 끊다→끊기다, 쫓다→쫓기다, 빼앗다→빼앗기다 (have it taken away). The agent, if mentioned, usually takes 에게/한테 for a person/animal (모기에게 물렸어요) or 에 for a thing/force (소나기에 옷이 다 젖었어요).
contrastWith: 이/히/리/기 passive vs -아/어지다 passive — the four-marker type is the fixed, built-in passive of a closed list of transitive verbs and usually names a clean event or natural happening: 문이 열렸어요 = the door opened/got opened. -아/어지다 attaches far more freely and leans toward a change of state or 'it does so by itself': 이 펜은 글씨가 잘 써져요 = this pen writes well. When a verb already owns a lexical passive, that one wins — the door 'gets closed' is 문이 닫혀요, NOT 문이 닫아져요. Also separate it from 받다/당하다 passives used with Sino-Korean nouns (사랑받다 = be loved, 무시당하다 = be ignored), which cover abstract 'receive an action' meanings the marker passive can't.
sentenceFrames: 여기서 ___이/가 잘 보여요/들려요 (You can see/hear ___ well here)

examples.ko: 글씨가 너무 작아서 잘 안 보여요.
examples.en: The writing is so small I can't see it well.
examples.note: 보다(see)→보이다(be visible); the thing seen takes 이/가, not 을/를.

examples.ko: 지하철에 사람이 너무 많아서 문이 안 닫혀요.
examples.en: There are so many people on the subway that the door won't close.
examples.note: 닫다→닫히다 (-히-): a natural 'won't close' event, no agent named.

examples.ko: 어젯밤에 모기한테 다리를 세 군데나 물렸어요.
examples.en: Last night I got bitten on the leg in three spots by a mosquito.
examples.note: Real-life complaint: agent 모기 + 한테, body part stays as 다리를.

commonMistakes: Guessing the marker. Each verb is married to ONE fixed marker, so 열다→열리다 (never 열이다) and 닫다→닫히다 (never 닫리다); there is no rule to derive it, you memorize pairs (보이다, 들리다, 팔리다).
Keeping 을/를 from the active sentence. In the passive the affected thing becomes the subject with 이/가: 문을 열려요 ✗ → 문이 열려요 ✓.
Double-marking the passive by adding -아/어지다 on top of a lexical passive: 문이 닫혀져요 ✗ → 문이 닫혀요 ✓ (닫히다 is already passive).

practiceItems.prompt: Make 열다 (to open) passive, present polite: 'The window opens'
Make 닫다 (to close) passive: 'The door is closed'
Say 'I can hear music' using 듣다→들리다

studyOrder: Learn the four markers 이/히/리/기 as a set, then memorize a handful of high-frequency pairs (보이다, 닫히다, 열리다, 들리다, 팔리다).
Practice flipping the object to the subject: 문을 닫다 → 문이 닫히다.
Add the agent with 에게/한테 only when you really need to say who did it (모기한테 물렸어요).
beginnerExplanation: Korean passives slip a tiny syllable — 이, 히, 리, or 기 — inside the verb so the action lands ON the subject instead of being done BY it. Mnemonic: picture the verb 'swallowing a pill' (이·히·리·기) and going limp — it stops acting and starts receiving. So 닫다 (to close something) becomes 닫히다 (to be closed): 문이 닫혔어요 = the door got closed. The catch is that each verb only ever swallows ONE specific pill, and there's no rule for guessing which — you memorize them (열리다, 들리다, 보이다, 팔리다). You'll hear these constantly: 안 들려요 (I can't hear), 안 보여요 (I can't see), 다 팔렸어요 (it's all sold out). Start with those everyday ones and the pattern clicks fast.

title: Causative verbs (이/히/리/기/우)
plainEnglish: Turns a verb into a causative one, meaning you make or let someone or something do the action.
whenToUse: Use this when YOU cause a change in someone or something — feeding a child (밥을 먹여요), waking someone (깨워요), seating a guest (앉혀요), stopping a taxi (세워 주세요), raising a pet or a kid (키워요), or turning the volume up (소리를 키워요). It is the daily language of parenting, caregiving, driving, and getting things done to others. 사동(使動) literally means 'cause-move', i.e. you MAKE the motion happen in another party. The one made to act takes 에게/한테 (or 을/를 for hands-on cases): 아이에게 약을 먹여요. Like the passive, this is a closed, memorized set living inside specific verbs — not a productive ending you can stick anywhere.
attachmentRule: Insert -이-/-히-/-리-/-기-/-우- between stem and ending; the choice is fixed per verb. -이-: 먹다→먹이다 (feed), 보다→보이다 (show), 죽다→죽이다, 끓다→끓이다. -히-: 입다→입히다 (dress someone), 앉다→앉히다 (seat), 눕다→눕히다, 읽다→읽히다. -리-: 살다→살리다 (save/keep alive), 울다→울리다 (make cry), 알다→알리다 (inform), 돌다→돌리다. -기-: 웃다→웃기다 (make laugh), 씻다→씻기다 (wash someone), 맡다→맡기다, 신다→신기다. -우-: 자다→재우다 (put to sleep; note 자→재), 서다→세우다 (stop/stand it up), 깨다→깨우다 (wake someone), 타다→태우다 (give a ride), 크다→키우다 (raise). The person made to act takes 에게/한테 or 을/를.
contrastWith: Causative marker vs V-게 하다 — the embedded marker (먹이다 = feed someone directly, spoon in hand) implies hands-on, DIRECT causation, while V-게 하다 (먹게 하다 = make/let them eat) is INDIRECT: you bring it about but they do the eating. 아이를 재우다 = I put the baby to sleep (rock it, lie it down myself); 아이가 자게 하다 = I make/let the child go to sleep (turn off lights, tell it to). Also keep the look-alike passive distinct: 울리다 from this list = MAKE cry (causative), whereas the verb 울다 alone = cry — same surface shape, opposite roles, sorted out by the particles around it.
sentenceFrames: 소리/값을 ___ -여 주세요 (Please turn up / lower the ...)

examples.ko: 아기한테 이유식을 천천히 먹여요.
examples.en: I slowly feed the baby its baby food.
examples.note: 먹다(eat)→먹이다(feed); the eater takes 한테, the food takes 을/를.

examples.ko: 아침마다 알람 두 개로 아이를 깨워요.
examples.en: Every morning I wake the kid with two alarms.
examples.note: 깨다(wake up, intrans.)→깨우다 (-우-): you do the waking to 아이를.

examples.ko: 기사님, 저기 횡단보도 앞에서 세워 주세요.
examples.en: Driver, please pull over there in front of the crosswalk.
examples.note: 서다(stop, intrans.)→세우다; 세워 주세요 is THE taxi phrase, vowel shift 서→세.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the look-alike causative and passive. 보이다 can be 'be seen' (passive) OR 'show' (causative), and 울리다 = make cry while 울다 = cry; the particles (이/가 vs 을/를, plus an agent) decide which.
Forgetting the vowel shift in the -우- group: 자다→재우다, 서다→세우다, 타다→태우다 — never 자우다, 서우다, 타우다.
Using V-게 하다 when direct hands-on causation is meant: telling a doctor you 'fed' the patient is 약을 먹였어요, not 약을 먹게 했어요 (the latter sounds like you merely got them to take it themselves).

practiceItems.prompt: Make 먹다 (to eat) causative: 'I feed the baby'
Use 자다→재우다: 'I put the child to sleep' (past)
Use 서다→세우다: 'Please stop the car here'

studyOrder: Learn the five markers 이/히/리/기/우, then memorize the most useful pairs (먹이다, 입히다, 재우다, 깨우다, 세우다, 키우다).
Notice which causatives look identical to a passive (보이다, 울리다) and rely on particles to tell them apart.
Contrast the direct embedded causative with the looser V-게 하다 so you pick the right nuance.
beginnerExplanation: Causatives add the same little syllables — 이, 히, 리, 기, or 우 — but here the meaning flips to 'I MAKE it happen to someone'. Mnemonic: the passive verb 'swallows the pill and goes limp', but the causative 'hands the pill to someone else' — you stay the boss, they do the action. 먹다 (to eat) becomes 먹이다 (to feed): 아기한테 밥을 먹여요 = I feed the baby. The -우- ones tweak the vowel, so 자다 (sleep) → 재우다 (put to sleep) and 서다 (stand) → 세우다 (stop/stand it up) — that 세워 주세요 is exactly how you tell a taxi to pull over. A few causatives look just like passives (보이다, 울리다), but the words around them clear it up. Start with feed, dress, wake, raise, and stop — you'll use those daily with kids, pets, and taxis.

title: Do in advance & leave done (놓다/두다)
plainEnglish: Says you do something and leave it in that finished state, often as preparation for later.
whenToUse: Use this when you finish an action ON PURPOSE and leave the result standing, usually as prep for later — booking ahead (예매해 놨어요), making food in advance (싸 놨어요), leaving the AC on (켜 놓고 나왔어요), or setting something aside for now (올려 두세요). The flavor is 'I took care of it so it's ready'. 놓다 (to set down) and 두다 (to place/keep) both literally mean putting something down — here that 'putting down' becomes 'leaving the result down/in place'. It pairs constantly with 미리 (in advance) and 일단/그냥 (for now). This is the deliberate, agent-driven cousin of the neutral state description V-아/어 있다.
attachmentRule: Take the -아/어 connective (vowel harmony like the present tense) and add 놓다 or 두다: ㅏ/ㅗ stems → -아 놓다/두다 (찾다→찾아 놓다, 사다→사 놓다); other vowels → -어 놓다/두다 (열다→열어 놓다, 만들다→만들어 두다); 하다 → 해 놓다/해 두다. Then conjugate 놓다/두다 freely (해 놨어요 from 놓았어요, 해 둘게요). In speech 해 놓다 often contracts to 해 놨어요. With a noun phrase you can also say 켜 놓다, 열어 두다, etc.
contrastWith: V-아/어 놓다·두다 vs V-아/어 있다 — 놓다/두다 keep an action's RESULT in place deliberately for later use (창문을 열어 놨어요 = I opened the window and left it open on purpose), while V-아/어 있다 just neutrally reports a state that exists (창문이 열려 있어요 = the window is (in the state of) open, no claim about who or why). Note the particle clue: 놓다/두다 keep the object with 을/를 (the actor is still in view), but 아/어 있다 takes the subject 이/가. Within the pair itself, 놓다 leans 'just did it / quick prep, ready now', while 두다 leans 'leave it sitting for a while'.

examples.ko: 표 미리 예매해 놨어요.
examples.en: I went ahead and booked the tickets in advance.
examples.note: 하다→해 놓다, contracted 해 놨어요; 미리 underlines the 'ahead of time' prep.

examples.ko: 에어컨 켜 놓고 그냥 나왔는데 끄고 올걸 그랬어요.
examples.en: I left the AC on and just went out — I should've turned it off.
examples.note: 켜 놓고 = did it and left it on; everyday 'left it running' regret.

examples.ko: 그 서류는 일단 제 책상 위에 올려 두세요.
examples.en: For now, just leave those documents on my desk.
examples.note: 두다 = leave it sitting for a while; 일단 pairs naturally with 두다.

commonMistakes: Wrong connective vowel — it follows present-tense harmony, so 열다→열어 놓다 (not 열아 놓다) and 하다→해 놓다 (not 하아 놓다).
Confusing it with V-아/어 있다 for a plain state: 'the window is open' is 열려 있어요, but 'I left it open (on purpose)' is 열어 놨어요.
Forgetting the spoken contraction and over-pronouncing 놓았어요; in real speech it's 놨어요 (해 놨어요, 사 놨어요).

practiceItems.prompt: Use 사다 + 놓다: 'I bought it in advance' (past, contracted)
Use 켜다 + 놓다: 'I'll leave the light on'
Use 넣다 + 두다: 'Leave it in the fridge'

studyOrder: Build the -아/어 connective first (same as present tense), then bolt on 놓다 or 두다.
Practice contracting 놓았어요 → 놨어요, which is what you'll actually hear.
Feel the nuance: 놓다 = did it and it's ready now; 두다 = leave it sitting for later.
beginnerExplanation: V-아/어 놓다 and V-아/어 두다 both mean you do something and then leave it that way, usually so it's ready later. Mnemonic: both 놓다 and 두다 literally mean 'put down' — so you 'put the result down and walk away', leaving it set up. Think prepping: 표를 예매해 놨어요 = I went ahead and booked the tickets. You make the -아/어 form (just like present tense) and add 놓다 or 두다, and in real speech 놓았어요 squishes to 놨어요. The two are nearly twins; 놓다 feels like you just did it and it's set, while 두다 feels like leaving it for a while. Don't confuse this with 열려 있어요 (the window simply IS open) — 열어 놨어요 means I opened it and left it open on purpose.

title: While still in a state (-ㄴ 채로)
plainEnglish: Means doing something while still in the state left by a previous action, often one you forgot to undo.
whenToUse: Use this when one action's result is still hanging on while you do something else — sleeping with the lights on (켠 채로 잤어요), walking in with shoes on (신은 채로 들어와요), going out with the window left open (연 채로 나왔어요), washing your face with glasses still on. The nuance is usually a bit careless, forgetful, or improper — 'without undoing it first'. 채(로) is a bound noun meaning 'the unchanged condition (something remains in)'; 로 marks it as the manner. It rides on the PAST modifier because the state must already be established before the next action overlaps it. Reach for it to narrate little oops moments where a state lingered the whole time.
attachmentRule: Attach to the PAST modifier form of a verb: vowel stem → -ㄴ 채로 (켜다→켠 채로, 자다→잔 채로), consonant stem → -은 채로 (신다→신은 채로, 입다→입은 채로). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ then add ㄴ (열다→연 채로). The 로 is optional — -(으)ㄴ 채 alone is also correct. It describes a maintained state, so the verb is usually one that leaves a lasting result (켜다, 입다, 신다, 열다, 앉다, 눕다). Not normally used with motion verbs like 가다.
contrastWith: V-(으)ㄴ 채로 vs V-고 — 신을 신고 들어갔어요 simply sequences two actions (put shoes on, then went in), but 신을 신은 채로 들어갔어요 stresses the shoes STAYED ON the entire time, with a nuance of 'without taking them off', often improperly. So 고 = 'and then', 채로 = 'while still left that way'. Also separate it from V-(으)면서 (simultaneous actions you actively do at once): 음악을 들으면서 공부해요 = I study WHILE actively listening; 채로 is not a second action but a frozen leftover state you're carrying through. And unlike V-아/어서 (cause/sequence), 채로 never implies the first thing CAUSED the second.
sentenceFrames: ___(으)ㄴ 채로 자 버렸어요 (I fell asleep while still ___)

examples.ko: 어제 화장도 안 지운 채로 그냥 잤어요.
examples.en: Yesterday I just slept without even taking my makeup off.
examples.note: Negative state 안 지운 채로 = 'in the state of not having removed (it)'.

examples.ko: 여기는 신발을 신은 채로 들어오면 안 돼요.
examples.en: Here you can't come in with your shoes on.
examples.note: 신은 채로 (past modifier) — the shoes stay on throughout, slightly improper.

examples.ko: 급해서 가스 불을 켠 채로 집을 나와 버렸어요.
examples.en: I was in a rush and ended up leaving the house with the gas burner still on.
examples.note: Real 'oops' moment: state (불을 켠) lingers through the next action 나오다.

commonMistakes: Using the present modifier instead of the past one — it's 켠 채로 / 신은 채로 (past form), never 켜는 채로 / 신는 채로.
Attaching it to a plain motion verb or an adjective (가는 채로 ✗, 예쁜 채로 ✗). It needs a verb that leaves a lingering result-state.
Reaching for 채로 when you just mean 'and then' two separate actions — that's V-고 (밥을 먹고 나갔어요), not 채로.

practiceItems.prompt: Use 켜다: 'I slept with the TV on'
Use 신다: 'Don't come in with your shoes on'
Use 열다: 'I left with the door open'

studyOrder: Build the past modifier first (켜다→켠, 신다→신은), since 채로 always rides on that form.
Pick verbs that leave a state behind (입다, 신다, 켜다, 열다) and practice 'doing X while still in that state'.
Compare with V-고 to feel the difference between 'and then' and 'while still left that way'.
beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 채로 describes doing something while a previous action is STILL left in place — usually a slightly careless 'oops, I didn't undo it' situation. 불을 켠 채로 잤어요 = I slept with the lights still on; 신발을 신은 채로 = with your shoes still on. Mnemonic: 채 means 'as it is / still in that state', so picture a freeze-frame — the first action got paused mid-result and you walked into the next scene without unpausing it. The key grammar point: it clamps onto the PAST modifier form (켠, 신은, 연), not the present. Drop it in when the state hangs around the whole time: makeup not removed, window left open, glasses still on. Koreans use it constantly for little forgetful moments.

title: Special honorific words
plainEnglish: A small set of completely different verbs you swap in to show respect, instead of just adding -(으)시-.
whenToUse: Use these whenever the person involved outranks you — grandparents, parents, teachers, bosses, elders, customers. Some LIFT the subject (계시다 = honorably be present, 잡수시다/드시다 = honorably eat, 주무시다 = honorably sleep), and one LOWERS you toward a senior (드리다 = humbly give/do for them). The split is the heart of Korean honorifics: 존경어 raises the other person, 겸양어 lowers yourself. You'll need them in any respectful exchange — greeting a boss (사장님 계세요?), serving a customer (도와드릴게요), asking an elder about a meal (진지 잡수셨어요?). They travel with the honorific particles 께서 (이/가) and 께 (에게): 부모님께 선물을 드렸어요.
attachmentRule: Memorize these suppletive swaps. SUBJECT-honorific (honor the doer): 있다→계시다 (계세요), 먹다/마시다→드시다 or the higher 잡수시다 (잡수세요), 자다→주무시다, 말하다→말씀하시다, 아프다→편찮으시다, 죽다→돌아가시다. OBJECT/humble (lower yourself toward a senior): 주다→드리다 (드릴게요), 말하다→말씀드리다, 묻다→여쭤보다/여쭙다, 보다(meet)→뵙다/뵈다, 데리다→모시다. The honored subject also takes 께서 (이/가 honorific) and 께 (에게 honorific): 부모님께 선물을 드렸어요. 계시다 honors a person; for a respected person's possessions use 있으시다 (질문 있으세요?).
contrastWith: Special suppletive words vs plain -(으)시- — most verbs just bolt on -(으)시- (가다→가세요, 읽다→읽으세요), but this high-frequency handful REPLACES the whole verb, so you can't say 있으세요 where 계세요 is required (할머니가 계세요, NOT 할머니가 있으세요 for a present person). Separately, watch the direction trap: 드리다 is HUMBLE (you giving upward) while 주시다 is HONORIFIC (a senior giving to you) — a teacher gives you a book with 주셨어요, but you hand it to the teacher with 드렸어요. Same English 'give', opposite respect-direction. Likewise 계시다 (subject is present) vs 있으시다 (the senior HAS something / a state): 할머니가 계세요 = Grandma is here, but 할머니가 시간이 있으세요 = Grandma has time.
sentenceFrames: 할아버지께서 진지를 잡수세요 (Grandfather is eating his meal)

examples.ko: 선생님 지금 교무실에 계세요?
examples.en: Is the teacher in the staff room right now?
examples.note: 있다→계시다 for a respected PERSON who is present; subject would take 께서.

examples.ko: 사장님, 제가 메일로 다시 보내 드릴게요.
examples.en: Sir, I'll resend it to you by email.
examples.note: Humble 보내 드릴게요 — you do the favor UPWARD; 드리다 lowers yourself.

examples.ko: 할머니, 진지 다 잡수셨으면 약 드릴게요.
examples.en: Grandma, if you've finished your meal I'll give you your medicine.
examples.note: Subject-honorific 잡수시다 (eat) + humble 드리다 (give) in one breath — raise her, lower you.

commonMistakes: Using 있으세요 for a respected person who is physically present — for a person you must say 계세요 (있으시다 is only for their belongings/states, e.g. 질문 있으세요?).
Using 드리다 when a senior gives to YOU. You receive from them with 주시다; 드리다 is only when you give to someone higher (선생님이 주셨어요 vs 선생님께 드렸어요).
Stacking -(으)시- onto an already-honorific suppletive: 계시다 and 주무시다 are complete, so 계시세요/주무시세요 in the sense of 'be/sleep' is wrong — just 계세요 / 주무세요.

practiceItems.prompt: Say 'The teacher is in the office' honorifically (있다→계시다)
Say 'I'll give it to my parents' humbly (주다→드리다)
Ask Grandpa 'Did you eat?' honorifically (먹다→잡수시다)

studyOrder: Memorize the swaps in pairs: 있다/계시다, 먹다/드시다·잡수시다, 자다/주무시다, 주다/드리다, 말하다/말씀드리다.
Learn the matching particles 께서 and 께, which travel with these honorific subjects and recipients.
Keep subject-honorific (계시다, 잡수시다) separate from humble (드리다, 뵙다) so you raise the right person.
beginnerExplanation: For most verbs you show respect by tucking in -(으)시-, but a handful of everyday verbs swap out entirely. 있다 becomes 계시다 for a person (할머니가 계세요 = Grandma is here), 먹다 becomes 드시다 or the very polite 잡수시다, and 자다 becomes 주무시다. There's also a humble side: when YOU give something to someone above you, 주다 becomes 드리다 (부모님께 드릴게요). Mnemonic — think of a seesaw: 계시다·잡수시다·주무시다 LIFT the other person UP, while 드리다·뵙다·여쭙다 push YOU DOWN; both ways the senior ends up higher. These come with their own particles 께서 and 께. Two traps: use 계세요 (not 있으세요) for a person who's present, and use 드리다 only when you give upward — when a senior gives to you, it's 주시다.

title: Probably ... so (-ㄹ 텐데)
plainEnglish: Expresses a strong guess or expectation, usually setting up a related comment, worry, or suggestion.
whenToUse: Use this when you assume something is likely true and then lean into a follow-up — concern, advice, a contrast, or an offer. 길이 막힐 텐데 지하철로 갈까요? (It'll probably be jammed, so shall we take the subway?) or 배고프실 텐데 이거 드세요 (You must be hungry, so please eat this). The whole point is the caring or hesitant SECOND half it sets up; it shows you're thinking ahead on someone's behalf. It comes from 터(expectation/intention) + 인데 (the soft 'but/and so' connector), so it literally frames 'the expected situation is X, and (in light of that)...'. It's warmer and more tentative than a flat prediction, which is why it suits worries and gentle suggestions.
attachmentRule: Built from -(으)ㄹ 터인데 (터 = expectation), almost always contracted to -(으)ㄹ 텐데. Vowel/ㄹ stem → -ㄹ 텐데 (바쁘다→바쁠 텐데, 오다→올 텐데, 멀다→멀 텐데), consonant stem → -을 텐데 (좋다→좋을 텐데, 먹다→먹을 텐데). PAST guess: -았/었을 텐데 (도착했을 텐데 = they've probably arrived). NOUN: -일 텐데 (학생일 텐데). It can end a sentence as a soft 'I'd expect... (but)': 맛있을 텐데. For a 1st-person plan that sets up a reason, Koreans normally use the sibling form -(으)ㄹ 테니까, not 텐데 (제가 갈 테니까 걱정 마세요 = I'll go, so don't worry).
contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ 텐데 vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요 — 거예요 simply STATES a prediction (비가 올 거예요 = it'll rain), while 텐데 wraps that guess in a 'so / but / I'm a little worried' frame that leads into another clause (비가 올 텐데 우산 챙겨요 = it'll probably rain, so grab an umbrella). Also vs its own sibling -(으)ㄹ 테니까: 텐데 expresses a guess about a THIRD party / external situation and sets up worry-or-suggestion (손님 많을 텐데 = the guests will probably be many, so...), whereas -(으)ㄹ 테니까 states YOUR own intention as a reason (제가 살 테니까 = since I'll pay, ...). And unlike -(으)니까 (a definite, known reason), 텐데 is guess-based and softer.
sentenceFrames: ___(으)ㄹ 텐데 괜찮을까요? (It'll probably ___, will it be okay?)

examples.ko: 지금쯤 도착했을 텐데 왜 연락이 없지?
examples.en: They should've arrived by now — why haven't they texted?
examples.note: Past guess -았/었을 텐데 = 'probably already happened (but...)'.

examples.ko: 주말이라 사람 많을 텐데 좀 일찍 나갈까요?
examples.en: It's the weekend so it'll probably be crowded — shall we head out a bit early?
examples.note: Guess (많을 텐데) leads into a suggestion (나갈까요?), the core use.

examples.ko: 먼 길 오시느라 피곤하실 텐데 좀 쉬었다 하세요.
examples.en: You must be tired from the long trip, so please rest a bit before we start.
examples.note: Caring 텐데 about the listener (+honorific 하실) softening advice.

commonMistakes: Spelling it 텐대 — it's 텐데 (from 터인데), the same -ㄴ데 connector.
Confusing the consonant/vowel split: 먹다→먹을 텐데 (not 먹ㄹ 텐데), 오다→올 텐데 (not 오을 텐데).
Using 텐데 for your OWN intention as a reason — for 'I'll do X, so...' use the sibling -(으)ㄹ 테니까 (제가 갈 테니까 걱정 마세요), not 텐데.

practiceItems.prompt: Use 막히다: 'The road will probably be jammed, so let's leave early'
Use 배고프다 + honorific: 'You must be hungry, so eat this'
Past guess with 도착하다: 'They've probably arrived already'

studyOrder: Start with present guesses (바쁠 텐데, 좋을 텐데) and add a worry or suggestion after them.
Add the past form -았/었을 텐데 for 'they've probably already ...'.
Compare with -(으)ㄹ 거예요 so you reserve 텐데 for guesses that lead into another remark.
beginnerExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 텐데 is how you make a confident guess and then lean into a follow-up thought — worry, advice, or a gentle 'but'. 길이 막힐 텐데 = it'll probably be jammed, and you'd add 일찍 나가요 (so let's leave early). Mnemonic: hear it as 'I'd EXPECT that... so...' — 터 is the 'expectation' and 인데 is the soft lead-in to your next remark. Use -을 텐데 after a consonant (먹을 텐데) and -ㄹ 텐데 after a vowel (올 텐데); for a past guess add 았/었을 (도착했을 텐데 = they've probably arrived). It's warmer and more thoughtful than a flat 거예요, because it shows you're guessing AND caring at the same time. Tip: when the guess is about your OWN plan, switch to its twin -(으)ㄹ 테니까.

title: Get done / become (-아/어지다)
plainEnglish: Makes a verb passive or shows a gradual change — something gets done, or a state comes about.
whenToUse: Use this for two everyday jobs. With ADJECTIVES it means 'get / become more ~' as a change unfolds: 추워지다 (get colder), 좋아지다 (get better), 많아지다 (increase) — 날씨가 추워졌어요. With certain VERBS it makes a passive that focuses on the RESULT or an 'it happens by itself' feel: 깨지다 (get broken), 꺼지다 (turn off), 켜지다 (turn on), 써지다 (get written) — 글씨가 잘 안 써져요 = the pen just won't write. 지다 here comes from the verb 지다 'to come about / fall into a state', so the form literally means 'the action/quality COMES INTO BEING'. It's the productive change-of-state passive, the free-attaching counterpart to the closed 이/히/리/기 list.
attachmentRule: Take the -아/어 connective and add 지다: ㅏ/ㅗ stems → -아지다 (작다→작아지다, 좋다→좋아지다), other vowels → -어지다 (만들다→만들어지다, 켜다→켜지다), 하다 → 해지다 (편하다→편해지다). With ADJECTIVES it means 'become/get more ~': 추워지다 (get colder), 많아지다 (increase). With some TRANSITIVE verbs it makes a passive of result: 켜다→켜지다 (get switched on), 깨다→깨지다 (get broken), 만들다→만들어지다 (get made), 쓰다→써지다 (get written). Conjugate 지다 normally (좋아졌어요, 깨졌어요).
contrastWith: -아/어지다 vs 이/히/리/기 passive — -아/어지다 attaches very freely and signals a CHANGE or 'it just happens on its own' feel (글씨가 잘 안 써져요 = the writing won't come out), while the embedded-marker passive (닫히다, 열리다) is the FIXED lexical passive of a small verb set. Crucial rule: when a verb already owns a lexical passive, that one wins — the door 'gets closed' is 문이 닫혀요, NOT 문이 닫아져요; double-marking 닫혀져요 is also wrong. For ADJECTIVES, only -아/어지다 works (날씨가 좋아졌어요), since 이/히/리/기 never attaches to adjectives. Separately, vs 게 되다: 게 되다 is about CIRCUMSTANCES leading to a situation (살게 됐어요 = I ended up living), not a physical state-change of the subject.

examples.ko: 날씨가 갑자기 추워졌어요.
examples.en: The weather suddenly got cold.
examples.note: Adjective 춥다(ㅂ-irregular)→추워지다 = 'become colder', a state change.

examples.ko: 휴대폰을 떨어뜨려서 액정이 깨졌어요.
examples.en: I dropped my phone and the screen got cracked.
examples.note: Verb 깨다→깨지다 = passive of result; focus is on the cracked outcome.

examples.ko: 한국에 오래 살다 보니 한국어가 훨씬 편해졌어요.
examples.en: After living in Korea a while, Korean has gotten much more comfortable for me.
examples.note: 하다-adjective 편하다→편해지다; 점점/훨씬 fit the gradual-change meaning.

commonMistakes: Using -아/어지다 where a fixed lexical passive is standard: the door 'gets closed' is 닫혀요, not 닫아져요; 'gets heard' is 들려요, not 들어져요.
Wrong connective vowel: 좋다→좋아지다 (not 좋어지다), 켜다→켜지다 (not 켜아지다).
Double-marking a verb that's already passive: 닫히다 + 지다 → 닫혀지다 ✗ → just 닫혀요 ✓.

practiceItems.prompt: Adjective change with 춥다: 'It got colder' (past)
Use 깨다→깨지다: 'The cup broke'
Use 좋다→좋아지다: 'My mood got better'

studyOrder: Start with adjectives + 지다 to mean 'become more ~' (좋아지다, 추워지다, 많아지다).
Add the passive-of-result use on a few verbs (켜지다, 꺼지다, 깨지다, 써지다).
Compare with 이/히/리/기 so you know when the fixed lexical passive is the natural choice instead.
beginnerExplanation: V-아/어지다 has two everyday jobs. With adjectives it means 'get / become more ~': 추워지다 = get colder, 좋아지다 = get better — 날씨가 추워졌어요 = the weather turned cold. With certain verbs it makes a passive that focuses on the result: 깨지다 (get broken), 꺼지다 (turn off), 켜지다 (turn on) — 컵이 깨졌어요 = the cup got broken. Mnemonic: 지다 means 'to fall into a state', so the quality or result 'falls into being' — it comes about, often on its own. You just take the -아/어 form and add 지다. One watch-out: some verbs already have a fixed passive (the door 'gets closed' is 닫혀요, not 닫아져요), so 아/어지다 isn't a free pass for every verb — but for adjectives turning into changes, it's exactly right.

title: Come to / end up (-게 되다)
plainEnglish: Shows that something came about by circumstances rather than purely by your own choice.
whenToUse: Use this when a situation LED to an outcome — you ended up doing something, came to feel a way, or things just turned out so. 회사 때문에 부산에서 살게 됐어요 (Because of work, I ended up living in Busan). It also politely softens your own decisions so they don't sound boastful or blunt, which is why Koreans use it for good news (붙게 됐어요 = I ended up passing) and for bowing out (못 가게 됐어요 = it turns out I can't go). 되다 means 'become', so 게 되다 literally frames the situation as 'it BECAME so that ~' — agency drains away from you onto the circumstances. It pairs naturally with cause phrases like 덕분에, 때문에, and -다 보니까.
attachmentRule: Attach -게 되다 directly to the plain verb stem with no vowel harmony (가다→가게 되다, 먹다→먹게 되다, 알다→알게 되다, 하다→하게 되다). Then conjugate 되다: most often past 게 됐어요 (= came to / ended up), also future 게 될 거예요 and present 게 돼요. ㄹ-stems keep the ㄹ (살다→살게 되다). It pairs naturally with reasons like 덕분에, 때문에, 하다 보니까.
contrastWith: V-게 되다 vs -기로 하다 — -기로 하다 is a DELIBERATE decision you made (가기로 했어요 = I decided to go), spotlighting your will, whereas 게 되다 DOWNPLAYS your agency (가게 됐어요 = it worked out that I went / I ended up going). Use the first for resolutions, the second for modest 'it just happened'. Also vs the plain past: 갔어요 flatly reports you went; 가게 됐어요 frames it as circumstances steering you there. And vs V-아/어지다: 아/어지다 is a physical/quality state-change of the subject (추워졌어요), while 게 되다 is about a SITUATION coming to pass (그 회사에 다니게 됐어요).
sentenceFrames: 덕분에 ___게 됐어요 (Thanks to that, I came to ___)
곧 ___게 될 거예요 (I'll come to ___ soon)

examples.ko: 한국 드라마를 보다 보니 한국어를 배우게 됐어요.
examples.en: Watching Korean dramas, I came to start learning Korean.
examples.note: -다 보니 + 게 됐어요: the most natural 'one thing led to another' combo.

examples.ko: 친구 소개로 그 회사에 들어가게 됐어요.
examples.en: Through a friend's introduction, I ended up joining that company.
examples.note: Circumstance (소개) drives it; sounds modest, not 'I chose to join'.

examples.ko: 갑자기 일이 생겨서 이번 모임에는 못 가게 됐어요.
examples.en: Something suddenly came up, so it turns out I can't make this gathering.
examples.note: Polite bow-out: 못 가게 됐어요 softens the cancellation as circumstance.

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before 게 — it's just 먹게 되다, 가게 되다, never 먹어게 / 가아게.
Using it for a firmly chosen plan when you mean a real decision; for 'I decided to', use -기로 했어요 (가기로 했어요), not 가게 됐어요.
Dropping ㄹ on ㄹ-stems: it's 살게 됐어요, 만들게 됐어요 (the ㄹ stays before 게), not 사게/만드게.

practiceItems.prompt: Use 살다: 'I ended up living in Korea' (past)
Use 알다: 'I came to know him' (past)
Use 못 가다: 'It turns out I can't go'

studyOrder: Learn the past 게 됐어요 first — it's the workhorse 'ended up / came to' form.
Pair it with reason phrases (때문에, 덕분에, -다 보니까) that explain how it came about.
Contrast with -기로 하다 so you separate 'it worked out' from 'I decided'.
beginnerExplanation: V-게 되다 says something came about because of circumstances, not just because you chose it. 한국에서 살게 됐어요 = I ended up living in Korea — work or life nudged it that way. Mnemonic: 되다 = 'become', so 게 되다 is 'it BECAME so that...' — the situation, not you, takes the wheel. You attach -게 되다 straight to the stem (no vowel changes) and usually use the past 게 됐어요. Koreans love it for two reasons: it explains how a situation unfolded (덕분에 합격하게 됐어요 = thanks to you I ended up passing), and it sounds humble, since you're not bragging about a personal decision. If you truly chose something on purpose, use 기로 했어요 instead; 게 됐어요 is for 'it turned out that...'.

title: Resultant state (-아/어 있다)
plainEnglish: Describes the ongoing state that remains after an action is completed.
whenToUse: Use this to say something STAYS in a finished condition: a door that's open (열려 있어요), a person who's seated (앉아 있어요), a package that has arrived and sits there (와 있어요), a sign that's posted (쓰여 있어요). The action already finished — you're describing the leftover result that's still true right now. It naturally pairs with intransitive and passive verbs (the ones that leave a state) and is the backbone of describing how a scene currently looks. Crucially it is NOT 'be doing' — Korean's 'be ~ing' for an action in progress is V-고 있다. Think of 아/어 있다 as a snapshot of the aftermath, not a video of the action.
attachmentRule: Take the -아/어 connective and add 있다: ㅏ/ㅗ stems → -아 있다 (앉다→앉아 있다, 남다→남아 있다), other vowels → -어 있다 (서다→서 있다, 열리다→열려 있다), 하다 verbs rarely use this. Works with INTRANSITIVE/result verbs and passives (가다→가 있다 = have gone and be there, 오다→와 있다, 죽다→죽어 있다, 켜지다→켜져 있다). For honor use 계시다 (앉아 계세요). NOTE: transitive 'be ~ing' is V-고 있다, not V-아/어 있다.
contrastWith: V-아/어 있다 vs V-고 있다 — 고 있다 = action IN PROGRESS (문을 닫고 있어요 = I'm closing the door right now), while 아/어 있다 = the RESULT-state after it's done (문이 닫혀 있어요 = the door is already closed). The particle shifts too: progress keeps the object 문을, the result-state takes the subject 문이. Also vs V-아/어 놓다·두다: 놓다 stresses someone DID it and left it on purpose (문을 열어 놨어요), with the actor still in view and the object as 을/를, whereas 아/어 있다 neutrally reports the existing state (문이 열려 있어요), no claim about who or why.

examples.ko: 문 앞에 택배가 와 있어요.
examples.en: A delivery has arrived (and is sitting) at the door.
examples.note: 오다→와 있다 = 'has come and is here'; the result of arriving lingers.

examples.ko: 벽에 '공사 중'이라고 쓰여 있어요.
examples.en: It says 'under construction' on the wall.
examples.note: Passive 쓰이다→쓰여 있다 = '(is) written and stays posted'; classic sign description.

examples.ko: 할머니가 거실 소파에 앉아 계세요.
examples.en: Grandmother is (seated) on the living-room sofa.
examples.note: For a respected person, 있다 → 계시다: 앉아 계세요, not 앉아 있으세요.

commonMistakes: Using V-아/어 있다 with a plain transitive verb to mean 'be ~ing'. 'I'm reading' is 읽고 있어요, never 읽어 있어요.
Wrong connective vowel/contraction: 앉다→앉아 있다 (not 앉어 있다); 서다→서 있다 (the 어+어 contracts, not 서어 있다).
Forgetting the honorific swap: a respected person seated is 앉아 계세요, not 앉아 있으세요 (있다→계시다).

practiceItems.prompt: Use 앉다: 'I'm seated on the chair'
Use 열리다: 'The window is open'
Use 오다: 'A package has arrived (and is here)'

studyOrder: Lock in the contrast with V-고 있다 first: progress vs. resulting state.
Practice with verbs that leave a state: 앉다, 서다, 눕다, 오다, 열리다, 켜지다.
Swap 있다 for 계시다 when the person in that state deserves respect (앉아 계세요).
beginnerExplanation: V-아/어 있다 describes the state that's LEFT OVER after an action finishes. 앉아 있어요 doesn't mean you're in the act of sitting down — it means you're already seated and staying that way. 문이 열려 있어요 = the door is open (someone opened it earlier and it stayed). Mnemonic: it's a photo of the aftermath, not a video of the action — the deed is done, the result is frozen in place. The big thing: this is NOT 'be doing' — that's V-고 있다. So 'I'm reading' is 읽고 있어요, but 'the package has arrived and is here' is 와 있어요. Use 아/어 있다 with verbs that naturally leave a result hanging around: arrived, seated, standing, open, turned on. It's everywhere in describing how things currently are.

hangul: 안 V / V-지 않다 / 못 V / V-지 못하다
romanization: an V / -ji anta / mot V / -ji mothada
title: Negation: don't vs can't
plainEnglish: Two ways to say no — 안/-지 않다 for simple negation, and 못/-지 못하다 for inability.
whenToUse: Use 안 / -지 않다 when you simply DON'T or WON'T (a choice, a fact): 오늘은 술 안 마셔요 (I'm not drinking today), 안 비싸요 (it's not expensive). Use 못 / -지 못하다 when you CAN'T — ability or circumstances block you: 운전 못 해요 (I can't drive), 야근해서 운동을 못 했어요 (I worked late so I couldn't work out). The short forms (안/못 + verb) are what you'll say out loud most; the long forms (-지 않다/-지 못하다) are a touch more formal/emphatic and are required in longer written sentences. A key Korean fact: 못 is for VERBS only (it's about ability to act), so adjectives can only take 안/-지 않다.
attachmentRule: SHORT form: put 안 or 못 right before the verb/adjective (안 가요, 못 가요, 안 비싸요). For 하다 ACTION verbs the negator splits the noun and 하다: 공부 안 해요 / 공부 못 해요 (not 안 공부해요). LONG form: attach -지 않다 / -지 못하다 to the plain stem (가지 않아요, 가지 못해요, 좋지 않아요). 못 is for verbs only (ability), not for adjectives — for adjectives use 안/-지 않다 (안 예뻐요). NOTE the pronunciation: 못 해요 sounds like [모태요], 못 가요 like [몯까요].
contrastWith: 안 vs 못 — 안 = you CHOOSE not to / it simply isn't so (안 먹어요 = I don't eat it / I'm not eating, by preference), while 못 = you're UNABLE (못 먹어요 = I can't eat it — allergy, too full, no time). Same verb, opposite reason. Short vs long form carries roughly the same meaning; -지 않다/못하다 is slightly more formal or emphatic and necessary in longer/written clauses. One more boundary: 못 + adjective is ungrammatical — 'not pretty' must be 안 예뻐요 / 예쁘지 않아요, because 못 only denies a verb's ability, never a quality.
sentenceFrames: 오늘은 ___ 못 가요 (I can't go ___ today)

examples.ko: 저는 커피를 안 마셔요.
examples.en: I don't drink coffee.
examples.note: Plain choice/habit: 안 + verb = 'simply don't', no ability issue.

examples.ko: 어제 야근해서 운동을 못 했어요.
examples.en: I worked late yesterday, so I couldn't work out.
examples.note: 하다-verb split: 운동(을) 못 했어요, never 못 운동했어요; 못 = blocked, couldn't.

examples.ko: 이 떡볶이는 너무 매워서 도저히 못 먹겠어요.
examples.en: This tteokbokki is so spicy I really can't eat it.
examples.note: Inability 못 먹다 (vs 안 먹다 = choose not to); 도저히...못 = 'just can't'.

commonMistakes: Putting 안/못 before the whole 하다 verb: it's 공부 안 해요 / 청소 못 해요, not 안 공부해요 / 못 청소해요.
Using 못 with an adjective. For 'not pretty' say 안 예뻐요 / 예쁘지 않아요 — 못 only negates the ability of verbs.
Mixing up the two 'no's: saying 안 먹어요 (won't, by choice) when you actually mean 못 먹어요 (can't, e.g. allergy) changes the meaning.

practiceItems.prompt: Say 'I don't drink (alcohol)' with short 안
Say 'I can't drive' with short 못 (운전하다)
Say 'It's not expensive' with long form (비싸다)

studyOrder: Master the short forms 안 V and 못 V first — they're what you'll say out loud most.
Practice the 하다 split (운동 안 해요, 운동 못 해요), the most common mistake spot.
Add the long forms -지 않다 / -지 못하다 for writing and emphasis, and remember 못 is verbs-only.
beginnerExplanation: Korean has two flavors of 'no'. 안 (or longer -지 않다) is plain negation: 안 가요 = I'm not going, 안 비싸요 = it's not expensive. 못 (or -지 못하다) means you CAN'T — you lack the ability or something blocks you: 못 가요 = I can't go, 운전 못 해요 = I can't drive. Mnemonic: 안 = 'I just AIN'T (doing it)' by choice; 못 = a wall (ㅅ at the bottom looks like a barrier) you can't get past. The classic trap is 하다 verbs: 안/못 squeezes in between, so it's 공부 안 해요 and 운동 못 했어요, never 안 공부해요. One more rule: 못 is only for verbs/ability, so 'not pretty' must be 안 예뻐요, not 못 예뻐요. Get 안 vs 못 straight and your 'no' sounds natural immediately.

title: Almost happened (-ㄹ 뻔하다)
plainEnglish: Says something nearly happened but didn't — a close call.
whenToUse: Use this for a NEAR-MISS — something (usually bad) that almost happened but, thankfully, didn't: 넘어질 뻔했어요 (I almost fell), 지각할 뻔했어요 (I almost was late), 가방을 두고 내릴 뻔했어요 (I almost left my bag and got off). It's the language of dodged little disasters and dramatic storytelling. Because a near-miss is already over, you'll basically always say it in the PAST as 뻔했어요. Pop 하마터면 ('very nearly / if I'm not careful') in front for the natural exclamation: 하마터면 ...-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 = 'I almost ...!'. It works with action verbs about events, not with adjectives or ongoing states.
attachmentRule: Attach to the verb stem: vowel/ㄹ stem → -ㄹ 뻔하다 (넘어지다→넘어질 뻔하다, 울다→울 뻔하다), consonant stem → -을 뻔하다 (죽다→죽을 뻔하다, 늦다→늦을 뻔하다). It almost always appears as past 뻔했어요 (= almost did, but didn't). Used with action verbs about events, not with adjectives. Often paired with 하마터면 ... -(으)ㄹ 뻔했다 (= 'I almost ...!'). 하다 verbs: 지각하다→지각할 뻔했어요.
contrastWith: V-(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 vs V-(으)ㄹ 것 같았다 — 뻔하다 means it GENUINELY almost happened and clearly did NOT (a real, physical close call): 넘어질 뻔했어요 = I nearly fell (lost my balance for real). -(으)ㄹ 것 같았다 is just 'it SEEMED like it would' — a guess or impression, with no claim it nearly occurred: 넘어질 것 같았어요 = it felt like I was going to fall. Also separate it from V-아서 큰일 날 뻔했다 vs a plain past report (넘어졌어요 = I actually fell, the opposite outcome). 뻔하다's whole point is the gap between 'almost' and 'didn't'.
sentenceFrames: 큰일 ___(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 (That almost turned into a disaster)

examples.ko: 길이 미끄러워서 넘어질 뻔했어요.
examples.en: The road was slippery and I almost fell.
examples.note: Cause + near-miss: 미끄러워서 (because slippery) → 넘어질 뻔했어요.

examples.ko: 알람을 못 들어서 회사에 지각할 뻔했어요.
examples.en: I didn't hear my alarm and almost got to work late.
examples.note: 하다-verb 지각하다→지각할 뻔했어요; everyday 'barely made it' story.

examples.ko: 하마터면 지하철에 가방을 두고 내릴 뻔했어요.
examples.en: I very nearly left my bag on the subway and got off without it.
examples.note: 하마터면 + 뻔했어요 = the natural dramatic 'I almost ___!' exclamation.

commonMistakes: Using the present 뻔해요 — a near-miss is finished, so it's almost always past 뻔했어요.
Wrong consonant/vowel split: 죽다→죽을 뻔했어요 (not 죽ㄹ), 넘어지다→넘어질 뻔했어요 (not 넘어지을).
Attaching it to an adjective or state (예쁠 뻔했어요 ✗). It needs an action verb describing an event that nearly occurred.

practiceItems.prompt: Use 넘어지다: 'I almost fell'
Use 지각하다: 'I almost was late (for work/school)'
Use 잊다 with 하마터면: 'I almost forgot!'

studyOrder: Learn it straight in the past as 'almost ...ed but didn't' — 넘어질 뻔했어요.
Add 하마터면 in front for the natural 'I almost ...!' exclamation.
Contrast with -(으)ㄹ 것 같았다 so 'it really almost happened' stays separate from 'it seemed it would'.
beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 is the 'I almost ___!' of Korean — a close call that, thankfully, didn't happen. 넘어질 뻔했어요 = I almost fell; 지각할 뻔했어요 = I almost got there late. Mnemonic: 'so close it 뻔-ished but didn't finish' — picture screeching to a halt one step short of disaster. Because a near-miss is already over, you'll basically always say it in the past as 뻔했어요. Pop 하마터면 in front to add drama: 하마터면 가방을 두고 내릴 뻔했어요 (I almost left my bag and got off!). Use -을 뻔했어요 after a consonant and -ㄹ 뻔했어요 after a vowel. It's super common in everyday storytelling about the little disasters you dodged.
